content: Group B Streptococcal (GBS) infection remains the leading cause of early-onset neonatal sepsis in the United States, despite significant advancements in prevention since the 1990s. Universal screening for maternal GBS colonization at 35–37 weeks of gestation and the use of intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis have substantially reduced the incidence of early-onset GBS disease in newborns. However, maternal GBS colonization rates have not changed since the 1970s, and continued efforts are necessary to sustain and improve prevention strategies. The absence of a licensed GBS vaccine means that universal screening and intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis remain the cornerstone of prevention. In the 1970s, GBS emerged as the leading infectious cause of early neonatal morbidity and mortality in the United States. Collaborative efforts in the 1990s led to the issuance of intrapartum prophylaxis guidelines by the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) in 1996, and by the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) in 1997. Revised guidelines in 2002 recommended universal culture-based screening of all pregnant women at 35–37 weeks of gestation to identify those requiring intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis. The most recent CDC guidelines were published in 2010. GBS infections can be classified into three main categories based on the affected population: pregnant women, neonates, and non-pregnant adults (primarily the elderly). Neonatal GBS infections are further categorized as early-onset (occurring within the first week of life) or late-onset (occurring after the first week, typically within the first three months of life). The gastrointestinal tract serves as the primary reservoir for GBS and is the likely source of vaginal colonization. Early-onset neonatal infections are acquired vertically through exposure to GBS in the vagina of a colonized mother. GBS is characterized by its ability to adhere to epithelial surfaces, penetrate host cell barriers, and evade the immune response. Its main virulence factor is the polysaccharide antiphagocytic capsule. GBS disease is caused by infection with the beta-hemolytic, gram-positive bacterium GBS, which is identified by the presence of the group B Lancefield antigen. It displays beta-hemolysis on blood agar plates and hydrolyzes sodium hippurate. GBS is part of the normal flora of the gastrointestinal and female urogenital tracts. The differential diagnosis of GBS infection varies based on the patient’s age and health condition. In neonates, early-onset GBS infection can present as pneumonia, meningitis, or sepsis and must be differentiated from other infectious agents. GBS primarily causes invasive disease in infants, pregnant or postpartum women, and older adults, with the highest incidence among young infants. Before active prevention efforts, approximately 7,500 cases of neonatal GBS disease occurred annually in the United States. Prevention activities in the 1990s and the recommendation for universal screening in 2002 led to significant declines in disease incidence. However, GBS remains the leading infectious cause of morbidity and mortality among newborns in the United States. Maternal intrapartum GBS colonization is the primary risk factor for early-onset disease in infants. Additional risk factors include gestational age less than 37 weeks, prolonged membrane rupture, intra-amniotic infection, young maternal age, and Black race. The CDC recommends universal culture-based screening for vaginal and rectal GBS colonization in all pregnant women at 35–37 weeks of gestation. Swabbing both the lower vagina and rectum increases the culture yield compared to sampling the cervix or vagina alone. Routine screening for asymptomatic bacteriuria is also recommended in pregnant women, with laboratories screening urine cultures for GBS at concentrations of 10⁴ colony-forming units (CFU)/mL or greater. GBS is the leading infectious cause of morbidity and mortality among infants in the United States, particularly preterm neonates. Most newborns with early-onset disease exhibit symptoms on the day of birth, while those with late-onset disease may appear healthy at birth and develop symptoms after the first week of life. Symptoms of GBS infection in neonates include apnea, cyanosis, cold skin, difficulty breathing, feeding difficulties, and irritability. In pregnancy, GBS infection is often asymptomatic. If symptomatic, the presentation depends on the type of infection caused by GBS. Physical examination of neonates with GBS infection may reveal lethargy, cyanosis, unstable temperature, tachycardia, and respiratory distress, which can manifest as nasal flaring, grunting, and tachypnea with intermittent apnea. Hypotension may also be present. In early-onset GBS infection, the 5-minute Apgar score may be low. Any newborn with signs of sepsis should undergo a full diagnostic evaluation and receive antibiotic therapy pending evaluation results, regardless of maternal GBS colonization status. Well-appearing newborns whose mothers had suspected chorioamnionitis should undergo limited evaluation and receive antibiotics pending culture results. Routine diagnostic testing for GBS is not recommended in well-appearing infants unless gestational age is less than 37 weeks or membrane rupture lasted 18 hours or more before delivery. Diagnosis is confirmed by isolating the organism from blood or cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). GBS infection should be suspected as a cause of bacterial meningitis in infants under two years of age, and empirical antibiotic therapy should be initiated immediately. Ampicillin or penicillin is recommended for confirmed neonatal GBS meningitis. Intrapartum antibiotic treatment should be administered to asymptomatic pregnant women who are GBS carriers to prevent transmission to the neonate. Penicillin is the preferred agent for intrapartum prophylaxis, with ampicillin as an acceptable alternative. Both are generally effective for treating GBS infection in non-pregnant adults. Penicillin-allergic women without a history of anaphylaxis, angioedema, respiratory distress, or urticaria should receive cefazolin. Antimicrobial susceptibility testing should be performed for antenatal GBS cultures in penicillin-allergic women at high risk for anaphylaxis. Clindamycin may be used if the GBS isolate is susceptible to both clindamycin and erythromycin, and testing for inducible clindamycin resistance is negative. Vancomycin is recommended if the isolate is resistant to clindamycin or if susceptibility to both agents is unknown. GBS vaccines have been investigated as a tool for reducing maternal colonization and preventing neonatal transmission, but no licensed vaccine is currently available. Phase I and II clinical trials of monovalent polysaccharide-protein conjugate vaccines have shown them to be well-tolerated and immunogenic. A recent trial of a conjugate vaccine against GBS serotype III demonstrated a significant delay in colonization acquisition among vaccine recipients.
